title: Getting an Answer Back: Futures, the std::async That Was Not Parallel, and a Failure the Caller Has to Handle

questions.question: Four tasks are started with std::async(std::launch::async, f) in a loop and the returned futures are not stored. Each waits up to 100 ms for the others. How long does the loop take, measured?
options: About 100 ms, since they run in parallel
About 200 ms
About 400 ms: each future is destroyed at the end of its statement and its destructor waits for the task, so they run one after another
Zero, since they are in the background
questions.explanation: Peak running at once was 1 with the futures discarded and 4 with them kept. Both gcc 11 and clang 14 warn about the discard as nodiscard, and the warning is the right one.

questions.question: A task submitted through submit_future throws runtime_error("sensor lost"). What does the caller see, and what does the pool report?
options: The pool reports failed 1 and the caller sees nothing
get() throws the same exception in the caller, and the pool reports failed 0, because the future caught the exception and kept it for the caller
get() returns zero
The process ends
questions.explanation: Measured: completed 2, failed 0. A plain task's failure is counted by the pool, lesson 07-10; a task behind a future delivers its failure to whoever holds the future.

questions.question: Why is the std::packaged_task held in a std::shared_ptr and the lambda given to the pool copies the pointer?
options: packaged_task is move-only and the pool's task type is std::function, which requires its target to be copy-constructible: measured, both compilers refuse it directly
shared_ptr makes the task run twice
To make the future thread safe
For speed
questions.explanation: There is still one task. Every copy of the lambda holds the same pointer. C++23's move_only_function removes the need; this curriculum is on C++17.

questions.question: A task is submitted to a pool that has already shut down. What does get() do?
options: Waits for ever
Runs the task on the calling thread
Returns a default value
Throws std::future_error with the code broken_promise: the refused task is destroyed unrun, and the future is told
questions.explanation: Measured: 'std::future_error: Broken promise'. A task dropped without running is reported to the person waiting, which keeps a refusal from becoming a hang.

questions.question: Why does the suite use ready_within before get()?
options: Because get() can only be called once
get() waits for ever on a task that never finishes, and wait_for never blocks longer than the limit you chose; measured, it gave up at 40 ms on a held task and said yes once it was released
get() is slow
ready_within returns the value
questions.explanation: Every wait in this curriculum has a deadline. A control path that waits for ever on a producer that has died has stopped controlling.

questions.question: What is the default launch policy of std::async, as measured here, and what does the standard allow?
options: On gcc 11 it ran on another thread, and the standard allows deferred, which runs on the thread that asks for the answer, so code must say std::launch::async when parallel is the point
It always runs on the calling thread
It always runs on a new thread
It is undefined behaviour
questions.explanation: std::launch::deferred ran on the calling thread, measured. The default is the library's choice, and a choice a program should not depend on.
